snippet.title: The Complete History of Coffee From Ethiopia to Modern Cafes
snippet.description:
Discover the complete history of coffee in this comprehensive documentary spanning over one thousand years. From its legendary discovery in Ethiopian highlands to modern specialty cafes, this is the entire story of how coffee transformed human civilization.
Journey through coffee's epic tale: wild Ethiopian forests, Yemeni cultivation, Ottoman coffeehouses, European Enlightenment cafes, colonial plantations, Brazilian dominance, American coffee culture, and the rise of Starbucks. Learn about the First Wave of mass-produced coffee, the specialty coffee revolution started by Alfred Peet, the Second Wave with Starbucks, and the Third Wave's artisanal approach.
This documentary explores coffee's dark history including slavery and exploitation, while celebrating the innovators who revolutionized how we drink coffee today. We examine modern challenges facing coffee farmers including climate change, disease, and economic sustainability.
Whether you're a casual coffee drinker or specialty coffee enthusiast, this educational documentary reveals the fascinating, complex, and sometimes troubling history behind your daily cup. From ancient legends to modern scientific innovation, from coffeehouses that sparked revolutions to the baristas perfecting latte art today—this is coffee's complete story.
Perfect for history lovers, coffee enthusiasts, and anyone curious about how this humble bean became the world's most beloved beverage.

snippet.title: Can we change the minds of science deniers? (Lee McIntyre, PhD)
snippet.description:
"How to Talk to a Science Denier" full video here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEiV9o6vwKk&

Think of it as the ultimate book club meeting...your friends and acquaintances show up to discuss a book, and the author shows up too!

From the book's website:

"Can we change the minds of science deniers? Encounters with flat earthers, anti-vaxxers, coronavirus truthers, and others.

'Climate change is a hoax—and so is coronavirus.' 'Vaccines are bad for you.' These days, many of our fellow citizens reject scientific expertise and prefer ideology to facts. They are not merely uninformed—they are misinformed. They cite cherry-picked evidence, rely on fake experts, and believe conspiracy theories. How can we convince such people otherwise? How can we get them to change their minds and accept the facts when they don't believe in facts? In this book, Lee McIntyre shows that anyone can fight back against science deniers, and argues that it's important to do so. Science denial can kill.

Drawing on his own experience—including a visit to a Flat Earth convention—as well as academic research, McIntyre outlines the common themes of science denialism, present in misinformation campaigns ranging from tobacco companies' denial in the 1950s that smoking causes lung cancer to today's anti-vaxxers. He describes attempts to use his persuasive powers as a philosopher to convert Flat Earthers; surprising discussions with coal miners; and conversations with a scientist friend about genetically modified organisms in food. McIntyre offers tools and techniques for communicating the truth and values of science, emphasizing that the most important way to reach science deniers is to talk to them calmly and respectfully—to put ourselves out there, and meet them face to face."

https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262545051/how-to-talk-to-a-science-denier/

snippet.title: The Uses of Delusion: Presented by Stuart Vyse
snippet.description:
Although reason and rationality are our friends in almost all contexts, in some cases people are better off putting reason aside. In a number of very important situations, we benefit by not seeing the world as it is, and by not behaving like logic-driven machines. Sometimes we know we aren’t making sense, and yet we are compelled to act against reason; in other cases, our delusions are so much a part of normal human experience that we are unaware of them. As intelligent as we are, much of what has helped humans succeed as a species is not our prodigious brain power but something much more basic.

In behavioral scientist Stuart Vyse’s new book, "THE USES OF DELUSION: Why It’s Not Always Rational to be Rational"  he looks at the aspects of human nature that are not altogether rational but, nonetheless, help us achieve our social and personal goals. 

Stuart Vyse, PhD, is a behavioral scientist, teacher, and writer. He taught at Providence College, the University of Rhode Island, and Connecticut College. Vyse’s book "Believing in Magic: The Psychology of Superstition" won the 1999 William James Book Award of the American Psychological Association. He is a contributing editor of "Skeptical Inquirer" magazine, where he writes the “Behavior & Belief” column, and a Fellow of the Association for Psychological Science and of the Committee for Skeptical Inquiry.

Views expressed in this talk are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Capital Area Skeptics.

snippet.title: Bunkers: The Cold War Plan for Surviving Atomic Destruction | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
For decades, humanity lived under the constant threat of nuclear annihilation. Hidden beneath forests, mountains, and cities across Europe, vast underground bunkers were built to survive the outbreak of World War III. From Soviet missile silos concealed deep inside Lithuania to secret West German civil defense command centers and East Germany’s heavily fortified communications hubs, governments prepared for the moment nuclear war would erupt between NATO and the Warsaw Pact. Massive concrete walls, anti-radiation systems, sealed airlocks, and underground control rooms formed part of a terrifying strategy based on Mutually Assured Destruction during the Cold War.

The documentary also uncovers Albania’s extraordinary bunker obsession under communist dictator Enver Hoxha, who transformed the isolated Balkan nation into one of the most heavily fortified countries on Earth with hundreds of thousands of bunkers scattered across the landscape. Through rare archival footage, former military personnel, Cold War maps, and access to once top-secret facilities, the film reveals how fear of nuclear war shaped entire societies and created underground worlds built for the end of civilization itself.

snippet.title: The First Roles We Were Given | Why Identity Existed Before Choice
snippet.description:
Identity feels personal. But for most of human history, it was not something you “found.” It was something you were given, enforced, and maintained by the people who needed you to be predictable enough to survive together.
In this Sleepless Homo episode, we go back before careers, mirrors, and self-help language. Before “authenticity.” Before even stable words for “me.” We follow identity where it actually begins in the record: in roles, routines, social pressure, and the quiet cost of belonging.
 You will hear how early humans likely became “someone” through repeated tasks, camp boundaries, learning windows in childhood, reputation, sanctions for drift, and the material signals that made membership visible. Not as a motivational framework, but as a deep-time survival system.

snippet.title: Not Exactly Lying: Fake News and Fake Journalism in American History (Prof. Andie Tucher)
snippet.description:
Fake news has marked American journalism since "Publick Occurrences" hit the streets of Boston in 1690, but an even greater danger is posed by the more recent phenomenon of fake journalism: the exploitation of the outward forms of professionalized journalism in order to lend credibility to falsehood, propaganda, disinformation, and advocacy. As the media have grown ever more massive and ever more deeply entwined in the political system, so has fake journalism, to the point where it has become an essential driver of the political polarization of public life. What happens to democracy when fake journalism looks more and more like truth, and fake truth like journalism?


Professor Andie Tucher, the H. Gordon Garbedian Professor and the director of the Communications PhD Program at the Columbia Journalism School, writes widely on the evolution of conventions of truth-telling in journalism, photography, personal narrative, and other nonfiction forms. Her most recent book is "Not Exactly Lying: Fake News and Fake Journalism in American History"  (2022). She previously worked in documentary production at ABC News and Public Affairs Television, and holds a Ph.D. in American Civilization from New York University. 

Views expressed in this video are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Capital Area Skeptics (NCAS).

For 100 years, the Presidents of the United States have been hiding serious illnesses from America. From an 1893 yacht surgery to today, the pattern has never stopped, and the constitutional amendment written to handle it has never been used.
This is the story of five presidents, five concealments, and the inner circles of doctors, wives, chiefs of staff, and press secretaries who decided what the country was allowed to know.

snippet.title: Why Humans Invented Rebirth | Trapped Between Lives
snippet.description:
Why do humans keep inventing “rebirth” across time, across continents, across completely different worlds?
 In this Sleepless Homo episode, we follow the oldest pattern behind transformation: separation → liminality → reintegration. Not as a motivational metaphor, and not as self-help, but as a calm archaeological and anthropological reality. Long before modern careers, “personal growth,” or identity branding, human groups built thresholds and enforced clean endings because partial change was dangerous. You were removed from ordinary life, held in a controlled in-between, and returned only when the group agreed you were real again. This is the liminal world between lives: caves, forest edges, rivers, outskirts, temporary ritual sites, costly ordeals as credibility tests, objects that function like receipts, burials that teach the living, renaming as social reset, and the keepers who supervised transitions so the group did not fracture.

localized.title: Why Humans Invented Rebirth | Trapped Between Lives
localized.description:
Why do humans keep inventing “rebirth” across time, across continents, across completely different worlds?
 In this Sleepless Homo episode, we follow the oldest pattern behind transformation: separation → liminality → reintegration. Not as a motivational metaphor, and not as self-help, but as a calm archaeological and anthropological reality. Long before modern careers, “personal growth,” or identity branding, human groups built thresholds and enforced clean endings because partial change was dangerous. You were removed from ordinary life, held in a controlled in-between, and returned only when the group agreed you were real again. This is the liminal world between lives: caves, forest edges, rivers, outskirts, temporary ritual sites, costly ordeals as credibility tests, objects that function like receipts, burials that teach the living, renaming as social reset, and the keepers who supervised transitions so the group did not fracture.
Sources are listed below in the description.

The United States was founded on a promise: no inherited power, no aristocratic class, no families above the law. The men who wrote that promise broke it almost immediately. Twenty-eight years after George Washington became the first president, the office had already passed from a father to his son. Two hundred years later, the same twelve families are still in the White House.

This documentary walks through the entire pattern.

snippet.description:

Every civilization on Earth independently invented dragons, despite never communicating with each other.
From Babylonian chaos serpents to Chinese emperors to Viking apocalypse myths, this is the complete history of the world's most persistent monster.

In 1922, Roy Chapman Andrews discovered massive bones in the Gobi Desert. The local Mongolians weren't surprised. They called them "long gu," dragon bones, and their ancestors had been finding them for thousands of years. This documentary asks the question: if dragons never existed, why does every culture act as if they did?

We begin in ancient Mesopotamia where Tiamat, the primordial sea dragon, was slain by Marduk to create the universe. We witness Egypt's nightly battle as Ra fights Apep, the chaos serpent who tries to swallow the sun. In India, we meet the divine Nagas, cobras grown to cosmic size who support reality itself on their thousand heads. China reveals dragons as symbols of imperial power, rain-bringing lóng who blessed rather than burned, claimed as ancestors by the emperor himself. Japan's eight-headed Yamata no Orochi terrorizes villages until Susanoo, armed with sake and cunning, cuts the monster down and finds a legendary sword in its tail.

The Norse show us dragons of the end times: Níðhöggr gnawing eternally at the world tree's roots, Jörmungandr encircling the ocean waiting to kill Thor at Ragnarök, and Fafnir whose cursed gold ruins everyone who claims it. We explore the fire-breathing zmey of Russian folklore, Wales' red dragon that became a nation's symbol of resistance, and Quetzalcoatl, the Mesoamerican feathered serpent who brought wisdom and wind. The dragon-slaying tradition reveals a pattern: from Apollo at Delphi to Dobrynya Nikitich to Saint George to Beowulf's final battle, heroes prove themselves by facing the wyrm. The documentary concludes by examining why we still dream of dragons in our movies, our games, our fantasies and what this 5,000-year obsession reveals about the human mind.

#DragonMythology #AncientHistory #MythologyDocumentary

snippet.title: Targeting Albert Speer: The Jealousy and Intrigue Inside Hitler’s Regime
snippet.description:
By 1942, Nazi Germany was losing the war it had started. The Blitzkrieg had stalled in the Soviet Union, the United States had entered the conflict, and Hitler desperately needed someone to save his war machine. Nobody expected him to choose his architect. Albert Speer had built Hitler's rallies and his chancellery. He had never managed a factory, designed a weapon, or run an army. But he had something nobody else in the inner circle possessed: Hitler's genuine friendship. And in a regime built on envy, that made him the most dangerous man in the room. What followed was two years of backstabbing, broken alliances, forged documents, and a power struggle so vicious it may have included an actual assassination attempt. All while the war was being lost around them. This is the inside story of Hitler's inner circle at its most desperate, its most devious, and its most self-destructive.

snippet.title: Great Moments In Evolution: The Journey From One Cell To Humanity
snippet.description:
How did life rise from a single cell to the astonishing diversity of animals, plants and humans on Earth today? This extra long evolution documentary follows the greatest turning points in natural history, beginning around four billion years ago, when life first emerged in the ancient oceans. One angle explores LUCA, Darwin, the Cambrian explosion, eyesight, intelligence, animal communication, sleep and Tiktaalik, the creature that helped open the path from water to land.

A second angle reveals how life survived catastrophe. Around 250 million years ago, Earth suffered its greatest mass extinction, wiping out more than 90 percent of ocean species and almost as many on land. Yet evolution continued, creating new predators, dinosaurs, eggs, sex, migration and the rise of mammals. From feathered dinosaurs and emperor penguins to CRISPR, mammoths and the threat of a sixth extinction, this documentary tells the ultimate story of survival, adaptation and life’s greatest inventions.

snippet.title: Melody Jue | Ocean Memory
snippet.description:
The ocean is not empty. It is a vast storage facility of memory agents. Ocean organisms use the chemical signatures of seawater for memory and intelligence in ways we can barely imagine. In her Talk, Melody Jue said our struggle to understand ocean memory comes from our terrestrial bias. This bias shapes what we try to protect and the technologies we develop. We must, she said, “deterritorialize the sensorium.” 

To better translate the ocean's memories, Jue worked with interdisciplinary artists, musicians, divers, and researchers to develop soundscapes that help us “smell” with our ears, remapping chemosensation through synesthesia. Don’t miss the moment in the Talk where she plays two original music pieces that use the density and flow of sound to mimic chemical gradients of seawater.

“The ocean teaches us humility,” Jue concluded. “It makes us confront our preconceptions about the planet and sensation.”

snippet.title: Complete History Of Imperial Japan From Origins To Defeat | Complete Documentary
snippet.description:
Journey through the entire story of the Japanese Empire, from ancient imperial myths and samurai rule to catastrophic defeat in the Second World War and the troubled legacies that still shape East Asia today.
This detailed documentary traces how the emperor became the symbolic core of the state, how the Meiji Restoration built a modern nation, and why Japan turned toward empire in Taiwan, Korea, Manchuria, and beyond. We follow the road into total war in China, the decision to attack Pearl Harbor, and the brutal Pacific campaigns that ended in atomic bombings and surrender.
Along the way, the video explains key turning points, ideas, and personalities, from reformist leaders and military strategists to resistance movements and ordinary civilians caught in the middle. Finally, we explore the Allied occupation, war crimes trials, Japan’s pacifist constitution, the postwar economic miracle, and ongoing historical disputes with neighbors.
Designed as an educational yet accessible narrative, this documentary is ideal for viewers who want a clear, fact based introduction to the rise and fall of the Japanese Empire and its lasting impact on the modern world.

snippet.title: Brown Gold Rush: Inside Madagascar's Violent Vanilla Trade | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
It is the second most expensive spice in the world, found in almost every kitchen in Europe, and it is tearing apart one of the poorest countries on earth. Madagascar supplies 80% of the global vanilla harvest, but while the price of a single kilogram soared from €35 to over €600 in just a few years, 92% of the island's population still lives on less than two euros a day. Behind the familiar scent of childhood and Christmas baking lies a world of violence, theft, corruption, and death. Farmers sleep in their fields to guard their crops. Lynch mobs patrol at night with machetes. A radio journalist has been kidnapped and threatened with death for simply reporting the truth. And somewhere in the chain between a Madagascan jungle and a supermarket yogurt, the question of who actually profits from the brown gold remains very difficult to answer.

snippet.description:

The shadow monster in Stranger Things has a name older than the show itself.
From Egyptian chaos serpents to Lovecraft's Nyarlathotep, this is the ancient mythology behind the Mind Flayer.

In Stranger Things Season 2, the Duffer Brothers introduced the Mind Flayer, a name borrowed from a 1975 Dungeons & Dragons monster designed by Gary Gygax. But the D&D creature was inspired by Lovecraft's cosmic horror. And Lovecraft was channeling fears far older than his 1920s fiction.

This documentary traces the Mind Flayer back to its deepest roots. We begin with the chaos serpents: Apep, who attacks Ra's sun-boat every night in Egyptian mythology; Azi Dahaka, the three-headed dragon bound beneath a Persian mountain; Jörmungandr, who wraps around the Norse world; and Tiamat, whose corpse became creation in Babylonian myth. These are the primordial shadows that predate order itself. Forces that cannot be destroyed, only held at bay.

We enter Lovecraft's world of cosmic horror and meet Nyarlathotep, the Crawling Chaos: a shapeshifting entity who possesses minds for entertainment, who walks among humanity spreading madness. We explore possession folklore from the dybbuk (Jewish soul that clings to the living) to Legion (the demon of the many) to Pazuzu (the Mesopotamian wind demon who possessed Regan in The Exorcist).

Then we examine real parasites: Ophiocordyceps fungus that hijacks ants' brains, making them climb to die in perfect fungal conditions. Toxoplasma gondii that makes rats lose fear of cats. Nature has always known how to steal the self.

Finally, we confront the hive: Greek bee priestesses who served collective consciousness, the Eleusinian Mysteries where ego death was sacred, and Jung's collective unconscious. The Mind Flayer is the terror of absorption. Of losing yourself to something larger that does not honor what you were.

A 2021 poll* of US adults asked, “In your opinion, how likely is it that the following [scenario is] true? The 1969 landing on the moon didn’t occur and was actually staged somewhere in Arizona.”

The results showed that 27% answered with “not sure,” “probably true,” or “definitely true!”

This poll isn’t an outlier.  It’s consistent with another poll** taken that year, showing 29% with similar responses!

Especially concerning is that these beliefs are more prevalent among younger generations, those born after 1980.

We skeptics have seen this situation play out again and again--an evidence-based rational claim is rejected by a sizable portion of the public, which instead supports an apparently absurd alternative explanation for the evidence.  What can we do?

Our next speaker has stepped up to the challenge.  On his own initiative, Marty McGuire (the “Backyard Astronomy Guy” of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania) examined the publicly available online science data compiled by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).  ISRO’s Chandrayaan-2 spacecraft has surveyed the Moon’s surface from orbit for several years.  In April 2021, it flew especially close to the Apollo 11 and 12 landing sites, obtaining the best images of those historic sites since 1969.

Mr. McGuire will demonstrate how he was able to (as anyone who wants to have a look for themselves can) obtain the raw images from ISRO and process them.  He’s shared the instructions and images across social media for the benefit of any other “do it yourself” researchers.  He and NCAS President Scott Snell (an engineer for NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter) will discuss this and other evidence of the Apollo landings.

Mr. McGuire, a marketing director for a community bank by day, is also a “NASA Solar System Ambassador” volunteer, communicating the science and excitement of NASA's space exploration missions and discoveries with people in his community.  By night he is an amateur astronomer, known online as the “Backyard Astronomy Guy.”

The views expressed in this presentation are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Capital Area Skeptics (NCAS).

* The Economist/YouGov Poll, “Belief in Conspiracy Theories,” https://docs.cdn.yougov.com/w2zmwpzsq0/econTabReport.pdf
** University of New Hampshire, Carsey School of Public Policy, “Conspiracy vs. Science: A Survey of U.S. Public Beliefs,” https://scholars.unh.edu/carsey/448/

snippet.title: The Entire History of Corinth 2 hours full Detailed Documentary
snippet.description:
Journey through the entire history of Corinth, one of the most influential cities in the ancient Mediterranean world. This full documentary explores Corinth’s evolution from its early mythic origins and powerful city-state era to its flourishing role under Rome and its dramatic transformations in the Byzantine and medieval periods. Discover how Corinth shaped Greek colonization, dominated trade routes, and played a decisive part in legendary conflicts like the Persian Wars, the Peloponnesian War, and the Corinthian War.

We dive deep into the rise of the Bacchiad oligarchy, the reigns of Cypselus and Periander, the city’s vibrant daily life, and its artistic innovations. Follow the destruction of Corinth by Rome, its rebirth as a Roman colony, and its emergence as an early Christian center visited by Paul. The journey continues through earthquakes, fortifications, Crusader rule, Ottoman control, and finally the creation of the modern Greek city shaped by archaeology and the Corinth Canal.

This is the complete story of Corinth, told with historical clarity, narrative flow, and rich cultural context. Perfect for history lovers, students, and anyone fascinated by ancient Greece.

snippet.title: The Origins of Werewolves - Mythillogical
snippet.description:
There’s a full moon on the rise, and so Charles and Cassie have bolted the doors, stocked up on silver bullets, and armed themselves with any knowledge on Werewolves they can find. Going all the way back to the Paleolithic, they search for signs of wolf men hiding among cave people, Proto-Indo Europeans, Ancient Greeks and Romans, the Norse, and the Medieval Irish, before investigating the infamous Wolf Trials from the 15th century onwards.

snippet.title: Stefan Sagmeister | Finally, something good.
snippet.description:
The world is terrible, and the world is better, Stefan Sagmeister said. Both can be true.

It all depends on perspective. In his Long Now Talk, Finally, something good, Sagmeister urged us to zoom out. The faster the news cycle spins, and the more we scroll, the more we catastrophize. Meanwhile, the things that improve tend to do so slowly and quietly.

In this visually stunning talk, Sagmeister takes us on a journey through his body of work, transforming long-term data on human progress into striking works of art.

This talk was presented February 17, 02026 at the Cowell Theater in San Francisco. 

Episode notes: https://longnow.org/talks/02026-sagmeister/

The event livestream is here: https://youtube.com/live/KXVf6lBxx1Q
    
This talk is part of Long Now Talks.

Launched by Stewart Brand in 02003, Long Now Talks has invited more than 400 leading thinkers to share their civilization-scale ideas with a live audience and millions around the globe tuning in to our podcast and videos. Long Now Talks are brought to you by The Long Now Foundation, which has spent the last 25 years igniting cultural imagination around long-term thinking.

By inspiring thought and conversation about how we've been shaped by the last 10,000 years and what might be in store for us over the next 10,000 years, Long Now Talks seek to expand our collective sense of the present moment. Long Now Talks cover futurism and speculative fiction; time, nature, and contemplative practices; the intersection of the humanities and sciences; the evolution of counterculture to cyberculture; cultural imagination, land art and public monuments; and of course, long-term thinking and being a good ancestor.

In our age of compounding crises, The Long Now Foundation is a counterweight. We are a force that imagines new possibilities, thinks critically, and takes action over the long term. We believe that when we all come together, bound by commitment and curiosity, audacious things become possible. Will you join us?  https://longnow.org/join

snippet.title: The Most Ancient Living Culture on Earth | Why Has This Story Endured 50,000 Years
snippet.description:
For over 50 millennia, Aboriginal Australia has carried one of humanity’s oldest continuous knowledge systems. This longform Sleepless Homo episode travels across deep time, uncovering how a culture survived rising seas, shifting climates, ancient migrations, early art traditions, language expansions, colonial rupture, and a quiet modern revival.

We explore:

• Ancient sea-level memories preserved in oral stories
• Dreaming cosmology as a living physics of land and law
• Rock art traditions older than the pyramids
• Ecological mastery through fire, water, and movement
• Genetic continuity stretching back tens of thousands of years
• Songlines as maps, libraries, and ancestral networks
• Encounters with Macassan seafarers
• Colonization, survival, and the hidden custodians who kept memory alive
• The modern revival of language, ceremony, and country
• A final reflection: What survives when time itself seems to fail?

This is not mythology.
This is archaeology, linguistics, genetics, paleoclimate, and memory woven together - told softly, for sleepless thinkers.

This lost civilizations documentary explores 126 archaeological mysteries that challenge everything we thought we knew about human history.
From Göbekli Tepe and the Great Pyramid to Angkor Wat and the sunken cities of the Mediterranean, witness the evidence that ancient peoples achieved far more than we ever imagined.
-
Twelve thousand years ago, before humans invented farming or pottery, someone built a massive stone temple in what is now Turkey. Göbekli Tepe shouldn't exist. It predates Stonehenge by 6,000 years. And it's just the beginning.

This documentary takes you on a 3-hour journey through the greatest archaeological discoveries ever made. You'll explore the engineering secrets of the Great Pyramid, dive into sunken cities like Heracleion and Pavlopetri, decode the mystery of the Bronze Age Collapse, and discover lost technologies that modern science is only now beginning to understand. From Roman concrete that strengthens over time to Amazonian civilizations revealed by LiDAR, each fact builds a case that our ancestors were far more capable than history books suggest.

snippet.title: The Real Kraken: Deep Dive Into the Most Feared Sea Beast in Human History
snippet.description:
🎬 WATCH AD-FREE & SUPPORT THE CHANNEL:
YouTube demonetized this channel but still runs ads on every video, meaning they profit from your views while I earn nothing. On Patreon you watch everything ad-free, and your support goes directly to keeping these documentaries alive.
➡️ Join here: https://patreon.com/FadingLore

The Kraken. For centuries, Norse sailors described something in the water: a body so large it was mistaken for an island, arms that could drag a ship beneath the surface, and an appetite for men. It appeared in royal manuscripts, in bishops' natural histories, and in the nightmares of every sailor who crossed the North Atlantic.

Then it turned out to be real.

In this documentary, we trace the Kraken from its earliest recorded appearance in the Konungs skuggsjá (c. 1250) through the scientific revolution that tried to classify it, the Newfoundland strandings that proved it existed, the writers who imagined it without ever seeing it, and the 21st-century expeditions that finally captured it on camera.

Featuring the real biology of the giant squid (Architeuthis dux) and the colossal squid (Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni), the failed and successful deep-sea expeditions of Clyde Roper, Steve O'Shea, Tsunemi Kubodera, and Edith Widder, and the cultural afterlife of a creature that went from myth to merchandise.
